Chapter 7: The Philosophy of the Fleeting Moment
Have you ever felt a touch of sadness when you realize nothing really lasts? Flowers wilt, seasons shift, even the closest friendships can slowly drift apart. But in the world of tea, that sense of impermanence isn’t something to shy away from—it’s actually something to welcome.
The Japanese have a beautiful word for this feeling: wabi-sabi. It’s all about finding beauty in things that are imperfect, fleeting, and unfinished. When you step into a tea room, this philosophy isn’t just an idea—it’s everywhere you look. The utensils are chosen not for their perfection, but for the way they remind us of change—a bowl with a tiny crack, a cloth whose color has softly faded, a branch of cherry blossoms that’ll soon let go of its petals.
Imagine being a guest in that room. Maybe you notice how the host has changed the decorations with the season. In spring, there’s just a single camellia in a rugged little vase. Come autumn, maybe it’s a sprig of red maple. Each detail is whispering to you: “Nothing stays the same.” And that makes this moment—this cup of tea, this gentle conversation—feel even more precious, because you know it’ll never come again quite like this.
Most of us, we race through life, holding tight to what we love, hoping we can somehow make the good things last. But the tea ceremony teaches us something different. It’s an invitation to slow down, to truly savor what’s right in front of us, even though we know it won’t last forever.
There’s a story that comes to mind—an old friend returns to the tea room after many years. The host greets them with that familiar, warm smile, but both know time has changed them. The tea still tastes the same, but the conversation? It’s richer, more tender. And as they say goodbye, there’s this deep gratitude—not just for seeing each other again, but for the sweet, fleeting nature of the moment itself.
Suddenly, it’s clear that impermanence isn’t some flaw we need to fix. It’s actually a gift. It sharpens our senses, makes us pay closer attention, and gently encourages us to let go of what we can’t hold on to. The tea ceremony, with its focus on right now, becomes a way to practice acceptance—it’s how we learn to make peace with change, and discover beauty in the flow of time.
A lot of people fall into the trap of chasing after things that last forever—searching for security, clinging to memories. But in the tea room, happiness is found in letting go, in trusting that this moment, just as it is, is enough. The chipped bowl, the flower losing its color, that quiet, honest conversation—these aren’t losses. They’re signs of life.
So, the philosophy of the fleeting moment isn’t just about tea. It’s really a guide for living. It reminds us that every day is special, that every meeting is one of a kind, and that life’s greatest treasures are often the ones we can’t keep.
